name: Stamford Bridge
summary: A crossing of the River Derwent east of York, guarded by a Roman fort, where Harold Godwinson surprised and destroyed the army of Harald Hardrada on 25 September 1066, and which afterwards remained a small Yorkshire village remembered for that one day.
overview: Stamford Bridge grew up where the road east from York to the Wolds crosses the River Derwent. A Roman fort stood near the crossing, the Norwegian army of 1066 chose it as the place to receive hostages from the whole of Yorkshire, and the death of Harald Hardrada there ended the last great Norwegian bid for England. For the rest of the Middle Ages it was a modest farming village beside a famous field.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Stamford Bridge is a village on the River Derwent in the East Riding of Yorkshire, about 11 kilometres east of York, where the main road from the city to the Wolds and the coast crosses the river. Its name is Old English: stan ford, the stony ford, with a bridge added by 1066, when the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle already uses the compound name of ford and bridge together.

A crossing on the Derwent mattered because the river, running south from the moors to the Ouse, divides the Vale of York from the Wolds. The place is famous for a single day, 25 September 1066, when Harold Godwinson caught the Norwegian army of Harald Hardrada there and killed both Harald and Harold's own brother Tostig Godwinson. For the rest of the Middle Ages it was a small village beside a battlefield that, according to Orderic Vitalis, could still be recognised half a century later by the bones left on it.

contentSections.title: The crossing before 1066
paragraphs: Archaeologists date a Roman fort beside the river to about AD 70, and a long civilian settlement later grew up along the road on either side of a Roman crossing about 1.6 kilometres south of the modern village. The road, known as Cade's Road, joined the fort to the network centred on the legionary fortress at York. The Antonine Itinerary places a station called Derventio seven Roman miles from York, a distance that fits Stamford Bridge, although antiquaries long gave that name to the Roman site at Malton further up the Derwent, and the identification is still argued.

Between the Romans and the Vikings the crossing is almost unrecorded. The river's name comes from a British word for oak, and some scholars connect it with Deira, the Anglian kingdom that became the southern part of Northumbria. By the eleventh century the Derwent lay in the earldom ruled from York, which Tostig Godwinson governed from 1055 until the Northumbrian rising of October 1065 drove him into exile, the grievance that brought him back beside a Norwegian king.

contentSections.title: Why the Norwegians came to the bridge
paragraphs: Harald Hardrada's fleet, some 300 ships by the Chronicle's count, sailed up the Ouse and anchored at Riccall, south of York. On 20 September the invaders beat the northern earls Edwin and Morcar at the Battle of Fulford, and York surrendered. Harald and Tostig took hostages from the city and demanded more from the whole shire, to be brought to them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September.

The choice of place explains what followed. Stamford Bridge was a road junction on open ground where men from across eastern Yorkshire could bring hostages and provisions, more than 20 kilometres from the ships, and the Norwegians went there expecting a ceremony of submission rather than a battle, leaving part of the army and much of its mail with the fleet. Harold Godwinson had marched north from London in about four days and reached Tadcaster on 24 September. He passed through York the next morning and came upon the Norwegians before they knew an English army was anywhere in the north.

contentSections.title: The fight at the crossing
paragraphs: The fighting is told in full in the article on the Battle of Stamford Bridge; for the place, what matters is how the river shaped it. The Norwegians caught on the York side were overrun and fell back across the bridge to the main body, which formed a shield wall beyond it. A passage added to the C text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in the twelfth century tells of a single Norwegian holding the narrow bridge against the English army until a man got beneath it and stabbed him through the planks; Henry of Huntingdon repeats the story, and later tellers put the attacker in a floating tub. It may be legend, but it shows that writers remembered the bridge as the choke point that bought the Norwegians time to form up.

Harald Hardrada was killed by an arrow in the throat and Tostig later in the day. Reinforcements who ran from the ships under Eystein Orre arrived exhausted and were cut down in their turn, and the Chronicle says the survivors needed only 24 ships to carry them home.

contentSections.title: Where the fighting happened
paragraphs: No excavation has fixed the site. The medieval bridge, of timber on three stone piers, stood a little upstream of the stone bridge that replaced it in 1727, and the stony ford may have been a separate crossing. The rising ground east of the river is still called Battle Flats, and the memorial stone for the battlefield overlooks it, but the Chronicle's words that Harold came upon the Norwegians 'beyond the bridge' can be read either way. The editor Charles Plummer argued that the phrase is written from the Norwegians' point of view, which would put the main fight on the York side, and Henry of Huntingdon's description of Norwegians driven back across the river over their own dead points the same way.

In 2020 metal detectorists working with a local heritage society reported Viking-age military objects on the east bank near Low Catton, about 1.6 kilometres south of the village, and argued that they mark the real battlefield. The finds have since been presented in a television documentary, but the claim rests on their interpretation and has not been confirmed by a published excavation.

contentSections.title: The village after 1066
paragraphs: Harold let the survivors go. Harald's sixteen-year-old son Olaf, who had stayed with the ships at Riccall, sailed to Orkney with Paul Thorfinnsson, earl of Orkney, and returned to Norway in 1067 to share the kingdom with his brother; as Olaf III of Norway he later founded, by tradition, the town of Bergen. Three days after the battle, on 28 September, William of Normandy landed at Pevensey, and Harold's army, weakened by its losses on the Derwent, marched south to the Battle of Hastings on 14 October.

The Derwent valley then shared the fate of the north. After risings at York and the arrival of a Danish fleet in 1069, William the Conqueror's army wasted Yorkshire through the winter of 1069 to 1070, and in 1086 Domesday Book recorded estate after estate in the county as waste. Orderic Vitalis, writing in the early twelfth century, said travellers could still recognise the field of Stamford Bridge by the great heaps of bones left by both armies.

Later medieval records show an ordinary village. Rents paid by its freeholders and cottagers were recorded in 1368, together with a common oven where villagers baked their bread, and Latin writers are said to have called the place Pons Belli, the bridge of battle. The crossing kept its value: the timber bridge on stone piers carried the York road until a new stone bridge designed by William Etty of York was built downstream under an act of 1724 and finished in 1727.

contentSections.title: Memory of the place
paragraphs: The Norwegian memory of the battle took shape in Iceland. Snorri Sturluson's saga of Harald, written around 1230, tells of a lone rider who offered Tostig his earldom back and offered Harald only a grave's length of English ground, a little more because he was taller than other men, and who turned out to be King Harold himself. The scene is literature, but it made Stamford Bridge a name every reader of the sagas knew. An English Life of Edward the Confessor painted around 1250 to 1260 pictures the battle in the armour of its own day, and Peter Nicolai Arbo's painting of 1870 gave Norwegian national romanticism its image of Harald's last stand.

In the village a memorial with inscriptions in English and Norwegian stands on the main street, and a second stone overlooks the fields thought to be the battlefield. Harold's victory there is measured by what came after: the English army that fought at Hastings nineteen days later had marched to Yorkshire and back and left many of its best men by the Derwent, so the crossing belongs as much to the story of the Norman Conquest of England as to the end of Norwegian ambitions.
